jsonld.name: Outdoor Flat-Top Fry-Up
jsonld.description: The café griddle, rebuilt outdoors: a flat-top plate (a camping griddle, a plancha over coals, or a steel plate over the fire) run in temperature zones, cooking four full breakfasts simultaneously the way the seaside caffs and bike-run burger vans have done for eighty years. This is the fry-up at its most social — everyone eats at once, the cook works a flat plane of heat like a short-order professional, and the plate's every component comes off the same seasoned steel. The flat-top's doctrine is zoning: the plate runs hottest over the flame's centre and cooler at its edges, and the cook assigns components by their heat needs — sausages and hash browns in the hot middle, bacon and black pudding at mid-heat, eggs, beans, and tomatoes at the cool rim. The zones replace the pan sequence; the plate's geography is the timing map.
recipeIngredient: 4 frozen or par-frozen hash browns (360 g), or 600 g potato wedges, par-boiled
300 g chestnut mushrooms, halved if large
30 ml / 28 g neutral oil, for the plate
1 tsp (2 g) brown sugar, for the tomatoes
Brown sauce and ketchup; a flask of tea or the billy on the corner

recipeInstructions.name: Step 1
recipeInstructions.text: Hot zone — sausages and hash browns, 12–14 minutes. Lay the sausages in the plate's hottest centre zone with the hash browns beside them. Turn the sausages every 3 minutes, rotating their positions like carousel horses so each takes its turn over the hottest spot; turn the hash browns at 7 minutes. Checkpoint: sausages browned all around with taut skins and clear juices; hash browns deep gold both faces. The hot zone's test: the first sausage laid down sizzles loudly within 5 seconds — if it whispers, wait; the zone is not ready.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 2
recipeInstructions.text: Mid zone — bacon and black pudding, plus mushrooms, 8 minutes. At the sausages' halfway mark, lay the bacon in the mid zone, pressed flat for 10 seconds each. Three minutes later, the black pudding slices join, then the mushrooms in the remaining mid-ground, cut-faces down. Checkpoint: bacon flat and glassy-amber; pudding crusted and holding; mushrooms browned faces-down, glossed. The zones are working when each component cooks at its own pace on the same plate — nothing burnt at the centre, nothing steaming at the rim.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 3
recipeInstructions.text: Cool rim — tomatoes, beans, and the bread, 6 minutes. The tomato halves go cut-face up at the rim with sugar and salt; the beans in a shallow pan or folded foil tray set at the plate's very edge, warming through; the bread toasts where the plate meets the air — its last heat, 60–90 seconds a side with a smear of butter. Checkpoint: tomatoes slumped jammy; beans bubbling lazily; bread golden with butter-freckles. The rim's cooking is gentle by design — the components there want warming and blistering, not searing.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 4
recipeInstructions.text: The eggs across the mid zone, 3 minutes. Clear the mid zone's cooked components to the warming plates. A fresh film of oil plus half the butter down, and the 8 eggs cracked straight onto the steel in two rows. Flat-top eggs are the crispy-edged master's method: 90 seconds undisturbed for lace, then a half-turn toward the cooler side for the last 30 seconds if the zone runs fierce. Checkpoint: lace-fringed whites, set and glossy, yolks liquid — eight at once, the flat-top's signature sight and the reason the method exists.

recipeInstructions.name: Step 5
recipeInstructions.text: The pass — four plates at the same minute. Off the plate in reverse order: eggs lifted last onto each plate's crown, then the works arranged around — sausage, bacon, pudding, hash brown, tomato, mushrooms, beans at the side, bread propped. Sauce bottles down the table's middle; tea poured. Checkpoint: four complete plates, all hot, all landed inside the same minute — the flat-top's entire justification. At a pan, the fourth plate waits; at a flat-top, the family sits. The plate scrapes clean with the fish slice and a splash of water while still hot — the steel's cleaning is its re-seasoning.

skeleton:
Outdoor Flat-Top Fry-Up

British · Medium · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The café griddle, rebuilt outdoors: a flat-top plate (a camping griddle, a plancha over coals, or a steel plate over the fire) run in temperature zones, cooking four full breakfasts simultaneously the way the seaside caffs and bike-run burger vans have done for eighty years. This is the fry-up at its most social — everyone eats at once, the cook works a flat plane of heat like a short-order professional, and the plate's every component comes off the same seasoned steel. The flat-top's doctrine is zoning: the plate runs hottest over the flame's centre and cooler at its edges, and the cook assigns components by their heat needs — sausages and hash browns in the hot middle, bacon and black pudding at mid-heat, eggs, beans, and tomatoes at the cool rim. The zones replace the pan sequence; the plate's geography is the timing map.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

For 4 plates

Fat and seasoning

- **Zones before food:** heat the plate 10 minutes and map it — a drop of water skitters and vanishes instantly at the hot centre, dances slowly at the mid-zone, and merely simmers at the cool rim. Push coals (or centre the burner) so the heat concentrates at one end; the gradient runs lengthwise. - **Season the steel:** a film of oil wiped over the hot plate with a paper towel (tongs-held) until it just smokes — the flat-top's non-stick is built, not bought. - **Everything in bowls, in zone order,** down the plate's cool edge like a mise en place buffet: sausages and potato at one end, bacon and pudding next, mushrooms and tomatoes next, eggs, beans, and bread at the cool end. - Four plates warming at the plate's far rim — the flat-top's own shelf.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • Zones mapped before food: water-drop test at three depths of the plate.
  • Hot zone: 12–14-minute sausages rotated to the flame; hash browns turned once.
  • Mid zone: bacon flat, pudding crusted, mushrooms face-down browned.
  • Rim: tomatoes jammy, beans lazy-bubbling, eggs lace-edged and eight-simultaneous.

Outdoor Flat-Top Fry-Up

Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 30 minutes · Total: 45 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

For 4 plates

  • 8 pork sausages (640 g), pricked once
  • 8 rashers (400 g) back bacon
  • 8 thick slices (400 g) black pudding
  • 8 large eggs (440 g)
  • 400 g baked beans
  • 4 frozen or par-frozen hash browns (360 g), or 600 g potato wedges, par-boiled
  • 4 medium tomatoes (500 g), halved
  • 300 g chestnut mushrooms, halved if large
  • 8 slices (400 g) thick bread

Fat and seasoning

  • 30 ml / 28 g neutral oil, for the plate
  • 40 g butter
  • 4 g fine sea salt
  • 2 g black pepper
  • 1 tsp (2 g) brown sugar, for the tomatoes
  • Brown sauce and ketchup; a flask of tea or the billy on the corner

Instructions

  1. **Hot zone — sausages and hash browns, 12–14 minutes.** Lay the sausages in the plate's hottest centre zone with the hash browns beside them. Turn the sausages every 3 minutes, rotating their positions like carousel horses so each takes its turn over the hottest spot; turn the hash browns at 7 minutes. Checkpoint — sausages browned all around with taut skins and clear juices; hash browns deep gold both faces. The hot zone's test: the first sausage laid down sizzles loudly within 5 seconds — if it whispers, wait; the zone is not ready.
  2. **Mid zone — bacon and black pudding, plus mushrooms, 8 minutes.** At the sausages' halfway mark, lay the bacon in the mid zone, pressed flat for 10 seconds each. Three minutes later, the black pudding slices join, then the mushrooms in the remaining mid-ground, cut-faces down. Checkpoint — bacon flat and glassy-amber; pudding crusted and holding; mushrooms browned faces-down, glossed. The zones are working when each component cooks at its own pace on the same plate — nothing burnt at the centre, nothing steaming at the rim.
  3. **Cool rim — tomatoes, beans, and the bread, 6 minutes.** The tomato halves go cut-face up at the rim with sugar and salt; the beans in a shallow pan or folded foil tray set at the plate's very edge, warming through; the bread toasts where the plate meets the air — its last heat, 60–90 seconds a side with a smear of butter. Checkpoint — tomatoes slumped jammy; beans bubbling lazily; bread golden with butter-freckles. The rim's cooking is gentle by design — the components there want warming and blistering, not searing.
  4. **The eggs across the mid zone, 3 minutes.** Clear the mid zone's cooked components to the warming plates. A fresh film of oil plus half the butter down, and the 8 eggs cracked straight onto the steel in two rows. Flat-top eggs are the crispy-edged master's method: 90 seconds undisturbed for lace, then a half-turn toward the cooler side for the last 30 seconds if the zone runs fierce. Checkpoint — lace-fringed whites, set and glossy, yolks liquid — eight at once, the flat-top's signature sight and the reason the method exists.
  5. **The pass — four plates at the same minute.** Off the plate in reverse order: eggs lifted last onto each plate's crown, then the works arranged around — sausage, bacon, pudding, hash brown, tomato, mushrooms, beans at the side, bread propped. Sauce bottles down the table's middle; tea poured. Checkpoint — four complete plates, all hot, all landed inside the same minute — the flat-top's entire justification. At a pan, the fourth plate waits; at a flat-top, the family sits. The plate scrapes clean with the fish slice and a splash of water while still hot — the steel's cleaning is its re-seasoning.

Finish & Plate

Family style down the table, sauce bottles centred, and the flat-top's theatre as the meal's opening act — everyone watching their breakfast cook is the oldest form of dinner-party entertainment. The plate cools, wipes, and re-oils for the next batch; a second round for late risers is 15 minutes' work on a seasoned surface.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Everything cooked at one speedNo zoning — heat even everywhereRake coals to one end; map with the water-drop before the food lands
Food stuck to the steelPlate under-seasoned or not hot enoughThe smoking-oil wipe; the 5-second sizzle test per zone
Burnt middles, raw rimsZones inverted — delicate food at the flameEggs, beans, tomatoes always at the rim; only sturdy foods over the centre
Second batch cooked unevenlySteel un-scraped, heat unmapped againScrape and re-oil while hot; re-map — the zone map shifts as coals settle

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Cooked components hold and reheat** on the warm plate's rim or a tray at 160 °C; eggs always cook fresh to order — the flat-top's whole point is that fresh is easy. - **Variation — the burger-van breakfast roll:** the flat-top's eggs and bacon in a floury bap with brown sauce, cooked at the cool rim for the queue — the method's most famous commercial form, reproduced exactly. - **Variation — the Plancha deluxe:** add 8 quail eggs at the rim for the mini-full-English plates' companion dish — 90 seconds each, the flat-top's most charming trick. - **The kit note:** any steel plate over any controllable heat runs this recipe — a dedicated flat-top, a cast-iron griddle, a plough disc. The zones are the recipe; the steel is just where they live.

methodSteps.chefsNote: a steel plate's heat recovery is the professional's hidden advantage and the home cook's hidden lesson: cast iron and steel pull their temperature down when cold food lands, but a thick plate's thermal mass restores the zone in seconds, while a thin pan sulks for a minute. If your home griddle is thin and the eggs knock the heat out of it, preheat it hotter than feels wise (a droplet's instant vanish) and the first eggs' landing brings it down to exactly right — the flat-top cook's oldest calibration trick, done by feel.
